title.en: Lhamo, the Goddess Who Rode on Her Son's Skin
title.zh: 吉祥天母：以兒皮為鞍的女神

region.en: Mountain Olkhan in the district Olgon, beyond the ocean Muliding (symbolic pin in the north-east)
region.zh: Muliding大洋彼端奧爾袞之奧爾堪山（以東北方為象徵定位）

texts.period: Paldan Lhamoi kang shag (Confession before the venerated Lhamo); Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: The goddess Lhamo was married to Shinje, king of the Dudpos, who at the time of the marriage had assumed the form of the king of Ceylon; she had made a vow either to soften her husband's notoriously wild and wicked manners, and make him favourably disposed towards the religion of Buddha, or, failing, to extirpate a royal race so hostile to his creed by killing the children that might issue from the marriage. Unable to improve the king's evil ways, she flayed her own beloved son alive during his father's absence, drank the blood from out his skull, ate his flesh, and using the skin as a saddle for the king's best horse, set out for her northern home. The king shot a poisoned arrow after her with a terrible incantation; she neutralized the imprecation, took out the deadly weapon, and uttered her curse-blessing: 'May the wound of my horse become an eye large enough to overlook the twenty-four regions, and may I myself extirpate the race of these malignant kings of Ceylon!' - and traversing India, Tibet, Mongolia and part of China in great haste, finally settled in the mountain Olkhan surrounded by deserts and the ocean Muliding.
summary.zh: 吉祥天母嫁與辛傑王（時化身為錫蘭王），曾誓：若不能感化此暴虐之王信奉佛法，便絕其惡王血統——親手誅其所生之子。她於夫王外出之際，活剝親生愛子，以顱飲血、啖其肉，以子皮為鞍乘王之駿馬北歸。王以毒咒射出毒箭，箭透馬背；天母破其咒，拔出利鏃，發願曰：「願馬背之傷化為巨眼，足以遍觀二十四域；願我親手絕滅錫蘭惡王之族！」遂疾馳印度、吐蕃、蒙古與中原，定居於 Muliding 大洋環抱之奧爾堪山。

texts.canonical_translation: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet, London 1863 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The goddess Lhamo was married to Shinje, the king of the Dudpos, who at the time of the marriage had assumed the form of the king of Ceylon. The goddess had made a vow, either to soften her husband's notoriously wild and wicked manners, and make him favourably disposed towards the religion of Buddha, or, failing in her praiseworthy endeavours, to extirpate a royal race so hostile to his creed by killing the children that might issue from the marriage. Unfortunately it was beyond her power to effect an improvement in the evil ways of the king, and, accordingly, she determined to kill their son, who was greatly beloved by his father because in him he had hoped to put a complete end to Buddhism in Ceylon.

During a temporary absence of the king, the goddess put her design in execution: she flayed her son alive, drank the blood from out his skull, and even ate his flesh. She then left the palace and set out for her northern home, using her son's skin as a saddle for the king's best horse. On his return, seeing what had happened, the king at once seized a bow, and, with a terrible incantation, shot off a poisoned arrow after his dreadful wife. The arrow pierced the horse's back, in which it stuck fast; but the queen, neutralizing the efficacy of the imprecation, took out the deadly weapon and uttered the following sentence: 'May the wound of my horse become an eye large enough to overlook the twenty-four regions, and may I myself extirpate the race of these malignant kings of Ceylon!'

The goddess then continued her journey towards the north, traversing in great haste India, Tibet, Mongolia and part of China, and finally settling in the mountain Olkhan, in the district Olgon, which is supposed to be situated in Eastern Siberia. This mountain is said to be surrounded by large, uninhabited deserts, and by the ocean Muliding. In a prayer addressed to this goddess she is invoked as Rimate - the present legend is related in the book Paldan Lhamoi kang shag, 'to perform confession before the venerated Lhamo', a treatise read when offerings are presented to this goddess, and a copy in Tibetan and Mongolian is in the library of the St Petersburg university, the Mongolian edition containing some details in Kalmuck which are not met with in the Tibetan.

The legend explains, in one stroke, the iconography and the office of Tibet's chief protectress: the flayed-skin saddle is the mule's pad she rides, the skull-cup of blood is the offering she drinks, the eye on the horse's rump is the wound of the poisoned arrow grown into the all-seeing eye that overlooks the twenty-four regions, and her permanent campaign against the malignant kings of Ceylon is the vow still operative whenever she is summoned from the north-eastern region surrounded by the ocean Muliding - by the blue letter Hum traced upon the suppliant's heart, spreading with its iron hook a beam of light, as the prayer has it. Schlagintweit identifies her with the goddess Okkin Tangri of the Mongolians, and with the Chammo or Lchamu of Pallas; her portrait, he notes, is found added to the picture of the thirty-five Buddhas of confession, and in Pallas's plates she stands beneath the central figure, sometimes without the staff and the skull-cup.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the legend explains the goddess's terrifying iconography - the flayed-skin saddle, the skull-cup of blood, the eye on her horse's rump - and her function as the wrathful protector who executed a dynastic vow to save Buddhism in Ceylon; she is identical with the goddess Okkin Tangri of the Mongolians.

functions: Explains the iconography of Lhamo's wrathful form: the mule's eye, the skin-saddle, the skull-cup of blood
Charter of theProtectress' vow: dynastic filicide committed to save the Buddhist dispensation
Localizes the goddess beyond the ocean Muliding, in the deserts of the north-east, from which she is summoned by prayer
The Paldan Lhamoi kang shag confession text is read when offerings are presented to her

region.zh: 梵天隱修之林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Drimed shel phreng (Spotless Garland of Crystals); Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: Tsangpa, a follower of the Buddha who had retired into the woods, was on the point of discovering the secrets of the Buddha doctrine by extraordinary meditation and the practice of virtues, when a Dudpo appeared before him in the shape of a beautiful woman who offered him exquisite delicacies; Tsangpa incautiously partook of them, was soon drunk, and in his phrensy killed the ram upon which the demon had ridden. By this savage act he lost the merits of the good works which he had accumulated with so much pain and perseverance, and attained no higher degree than that of a common follower, or Upasaka - filled with rage towards the evil spirits, he took an awful oath in the hands of the Buddha Vajradhara, vowing to do his utmost to extirpate the pernicious race through which he had lost his position.
summary.zh: 梵天（Tsangpa）本為精修佛法之隱士，將以禪定與持戒窺得佛道之秘；一魔忽化作美婦，獻上珍饈。梵天誤食而醉，狂亂中殺死魔所乘之羊——由此暴行，盡喪苦修功德，僅得「近事男」（優婆塞）之位。他憤而於金剛持佛前立下重誓：必竭力翦滅使其失位之惡魔之族。

sensitivity.note: Living pantheon tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

title.en: Chakdor and the Thief of the Water of Life
title.zh: 金剛手與偷飲不死甘露者

region.en: Mount Meru and the ocean of milk (cosmic, symbolic pin at the meridian of Meru)
region.zh: 須彌山與乳海（宇宙圖景，以須彌山為象徵定位）

texts.period: Drimed shel phreng (Spotless Garland of Crystals); Schlagintweit's English 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: The Buddhas met on the top of Mount Meru to procure the water of life, Dutsi, concealed at the bottom of the deep ocean, as a powerful antidote against the poison Hala-hala the evil demons were using against mankind; they churned the ocean with the mountain Meru, and delivered the water of life to Vajrapani to secure safely. But the monster Rahu, a Lhamayin, watched his movements, seized his absence to drink the water of life - and voided his water deliberately into the vessel. Fleeing past the sun and moon, whom he menaced with vengeance should they betray him, he was betrayed by the candid moon, overtaken, and struck by Vajrapani's sceptre so that his body was split in two, the legs blown off; forced by the Buddhas to drink the fouled water as punishment, his fair yellow complexion turned dark, and the Buddhas made a horrible monster of him: his legs replaced by the tail of a dragon, nine different heads formed from his broken one, the principal wounds made into an enormous throat and the lesser ones into so many eyes. His rage turned especially against the sun and the moon: he overshadows them trying to devour them, and thus causes eclipses - but owing to Vajrapani's unceasing vigilance he cannot succeed in destroying them.
summary.zh: 諸佛會於須彌山頂，欲取深海之底所藏的不死甘露，以解諸魔施於人間的劇毒「黑哈利」；遂攪乳海，令甘露上浮，交金剛手菩薩（Chakdor）看管。怪物羅睺（Lhamayin）窺其行止，乘其不在，偷飲甘露，更故意向缽中小解。逃遁時他威嚇日月不得告密；月亮直言相告，羅睺旋即被追及——金剛手一杵擊下，其身斷為兩截，雙腿飛散。諸佛又命他飲下被污之水作為懲罰，其金黃膚色遂變為黝黑；諸佛更將其化為怪物：雙腿代以龍尾，殘首化為九頭，主傷成巨喉，餘創化為眾眼。自此羅睺專仇日月，每欲吞之——是為日月蝕之由；然因金剛手時時警衛，終不能滅。

texts.canonical_translation: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet, London 1863 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Once upon a time the Buddhas all met together on the top of Mount Meru, to deliberate upon the means of procuring the water of life, Dutsi, which lies concealed at the bottom of the deep ocean. In their benevolence they intended, as soon as they obtained possession of the water of life, to distribute it amongst the human race as a powerful antidote against the strong poison Hala-hala, which the evil demons, at this period, had been using with such mischievous effect against mankind. In order to procure the antidote they determined to churn the ocean with the mountain Meru, and so cause the water of life to rise to the surface of the sea. This they did, and delivered the water of life to Vajrapani, with orders to secure it safely until a future meeting, when they would impart it to living beings.

But the monster Rahu, a Lhamayin, happened to hear of this precious discovery, and having carefully watched Vajrapani's movements, seized an opportunity, in the absence of the latter, to drink the water of life; not satisfied with this act, he even voided his water deliberately into the vessel. He then hurried away as fast as possible, and had already proceeded a great distance, when Vajrapani came home, and having perceived the theft, instantly set out in pursuit of the culprit. In the course of his flight Rahu had passed the sun and the moon, whom he menaced with vengeance should they venture to betray him to Vajrapani. His searches proving fruitless, Vajrapani betook himself to the sun, and asked him about Rahu; but the sun replied evasively, saying that he had certainly seen somebody passing a long time ago, but had paid no particular attention as to who it was. The moon, on the other hand, returned a candid answer, only requesting that Vajrapani would not repeat it before Rahu. Upon this information Rahu was shortly afterwards overtaken, when he got such a terrible blow from Vajrapani's sceptre that, besides receiving many wounds, his body was split into two parts, the lower part of the body with the legs being entirely blown off.

The Buddhas once more held a meeting, in which they deliberated upon the best means of disposing of Rahu's urine: to pour it out would have been most dangerous for living beings, as it contained a large quantity of the poison Hala-hala; they therefore determined that Vajrapani should drink it, in just punishment for the carelessness through which the water of life had been lost. Accordingly he was forced to do so, when his fair, yellow complexion was changed by the effects of this dangerous potion into a dark one. Vajrapani conceived, from his transfiguration, a most violent rage against all evil demons, and in particular against Rahu, who, notwithstanding his deadly wounds, was prevented from dying by the water of life. This powerful water, however, dropped from his wounds and fell all over the world, numerous medicinal herbs springing up on the spots where it touched the soil. A severe punishment was also inflicted upon Rahu by the Buddhas themselves: they made a horrible monster of him, replaced his legs by the tail of a dragon, formed nine different heads from his broken one, the principal wounds were made into an enormous throat, and the lesser ones changed into so many eyes. Rahu became, after this transformation, more dreadful than he was before; his rage was turned especially towards the sun and the moon, who had betrayed him. He is constantly trying to devour them, particularly the moon, who displayed the most hostile disposition towards him; he overshadows them whilst trying to devour them, and thus causes eclipses, but owing to Vajrapani's unceasing vigilance he cannot succeed in destroying them.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the Tibetan redaction of the Hindu churning-of-the-ocean, transformed into an etiology of eclipses and of Vajrapani's dark complexion; Schlagintweit notes it derives almost without alteration from Hindu tales, where Vishnu severed Rahu's head and the nectar secured his immortality.

functions: Etiology of eclipses: Rahu, unable to die because of the amrita, forever pursues sun and moon in revenge
Charter of Vajrapani's dark form and his permanent office as guardian against the sun-devourer
Explains medicinal herbs as the drops of life-water fallen from Rahu's wounds all over the world
Demonstrates the rule that the gods who cause existence simultaneously bring its destructive power into action

variants.name: The Hindu churning of the ocean
variants.summary: In the Hindu versions the amrita was also procured by churning the ocean; Rahu, a monster with a dragon's tail, disguised himself like one of the gods and received a portion; his fraud discovered by the sun and moon, Vishnu severed his head, but the nectarean fluid secured his immortality.

variants.name: Rahu's mythical measurements
variants.text_tradition: Singhalese books (Spence Hardy's Manual of Buddhism)
variants.summary: Rahu is 76,000 miles high, 19,000 broad across the shoulders, his head 14,500 miles round, his mouth 3,200 miles in size - and with one finger he can cover the sun or moon so as to obscure their light.

region.en: Pantheon of protective deities (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 護法神殿（以拉薩為象徵定位）

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: To subdue the evil spirits is one of the most important duties of the gods and genii, and they assume a horrible aspect when fighting with them, becoming highly inflamed with rage; a particular class have especially devoted themselves to the extirpation of evil spirits, further confirmed by an awful oath deposited in the hands of the Buddha Vajradhara - these are called Dragsheds, 'the cruel hangmen', and their anger against the evil spirits, so the legends relate, arose in consequence of the innumerable tricks that had been played off upon them by the latter. Amongst the Dragsheds the one called Yab yum chudpa, 'the father embracing his mother', is in addition able to deliver man from his sins if he sincerely repents and confesses them prostrate before his image - representations showing him with a female tenderly clasped round his body.
summary.zh: 降伏惡靈乃神祇之要務，臨陣時彼等現可怖之相，怒焰熾燃；有一類神專司翦滅惡靈，更於金剛持佛前立下重誓——是稱「Dragshed」，意為「兇殘之劊子手」。傳說其憤怒之由，乃因惡靈曾以千般詭計戲弄於彼。其中有名「父母相擁」（Yab yum chudpa）者，不僅能拒惡靈於外，亦能赦人之罪——只要人真心悔罪、於其像前伏地懺悔。其像皆作男女相擁狀。

title.en: The Dudpos and the Prolonged Bardo
title.zh: 辛傑之吏與延長的中陰

region.en: Region Paranirmita-Vasavartin, highest of the desire-worlds (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 他化自在天（欲界之頂，象徵定位）

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: The Dudpos, the assistants of Shinje the judge of the dead, inhabit the region Paranirmita Vasavartin, the highest in the world of desire; they try to hinder the depopulation of the world by supporting man in evil desire, and by keeping off the Bodhisattvas from attaining the Bodhi - it is they who disturb the devoutness of assembled Buddhists, and put an end to steady meditation by assuming the shape of a beautiful woman, or by suggesting ludicrous ideas, asserting that those who do not enjoy the pleasures of life shall be re-born in hell. But they are also those spirits who, when the time of death has arrived, seize the released soul and bring it before Shinje to be tried and sentenced according to its works. That death is considered untimely which, in opposition to the ordinary course of nature, is accelerated by the evil spirits; as a consequence the Bardo - the middle state between death and rebirth - is prolongated, and the wretched souls seized by the spirits appear to men as a raw, shapeless piece of meat, a vision considered unlucky, boding illness and even death.
summary.zh: 辛傑（閻魔）之吏「Dudpo」居於欲界之頂他化自在天；他們助長人的惡欲、阻菩薩證道，擾亂僧眾的誠敬，又化作美婦、出以諧謔，令修定者失其正念——並謂「不享人生之樂者將生地獄」。而人命終之時，亦是彼等抓住離體之魂，押至辛傑王前依業受審。凡為惡靈所催而違乎自然之壽，謂之「橫死」；橫死者中陰延長——此即死後與轉生之間的中間態；為靈所執之魂現於人前，狀如一塊無形生肉，見者大凶，主疾病乃至死亡。

title.en: Om Mani Padme Hum: The Six-Syllable Prayer
title.zh: 六字真言：唵嘛呢叭咪吽

region.en: Prayer-wheels and walls of all Tibet (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 全藏轉經筒與嘛呢牆（以拉薩為象徵定位）

texts.period: Six-syllable formula attributed to Padmapani; Schlagintweit's notice 1863

source.work: Emil Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863), ch. X

summary.en: Om mani padme hum - O the Jewel in the Lotus, Amen - is an invocation of Padmapani, who is believed to have delivered it to the Tibetans; it is the most frequently repeated of all prayers, and to each syllable is attributed a special magical faculty. In a prayer cylinder which Schlagintweit opened he found the sentence printed in six lines and repeated innumerable times upon a leaf 49 feet long and four inches broad; when Baron Schilling de Canstadt visited the temple Subulin in Siberia the Lamas were preparing 100 millions of copies of this prayer to be put into a prayer cylinder, and accepted his offer to have the necessary number executed at St. Petersburg - presenting him in return with an edition of the Kanjur of about 40,000 sheets. When engraved upon the slabs resting on prayer walls the letters are often so combined as to form an anagram, called in Tibetan Nam chu vangdan, 'the ten entirely powerful', and the power of the sacred sentence is supposed to be increased by its being written in this form.
summary.zh: 「唵嘛呢叭咪吽」——觀音（蓮華手）親授藏人之六字真言，為最常誦之咒。每字皆具別持神力。施拉金特魏特所開轉經筒中，六字凡四十九英尺長之紙上重複無數；希林伯爵在布里亞特寺院見僧眾備一億份以裝經筒，遂允代製，寺方回贈《甘珠爾》全藏（約四萬頁）。嘛呢石上六字常合為一個「十相自在」（Nam chu vangdan）符形，云其力更增。

passages.text: Om mani padme hum, O the Jewel in the Lotus, Amen, is an invocation of Padmapani, who is believed to have delivered it to the Tibetans; it is the most frequently repeated of all prayers, and has on this account excited the curiosity of the earliest visitors to Tibet. To each syllable of the prayer is attributed a special magical faculty, and in a prayer cylinder which I had the opportunity of opening I found the sentence printed in six lines and repeated innumerable times upon a leaf 49 feet long and 4 inches broad.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Schlagintweit, Buddhism in Tibet (1863); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Baron Schilling de Canstadt paid a visit to the temple Subulin in Siberia, the Lamas were just occupied with preparing 100 millions of copies of this prayer to be put into a prayer cylinder; his offer to have the necessary number executed at St. Petersburg was most readily accepted, and he was presented, in return for the 150 millions of copies he forwarded to them, with an edition of the Kanjur, the sheets of which amount to about 40,000. When engraved upon the slabs resting on the prayer walls, the letters are often so combined as to form an anagram, called in Tibetan Nam chu vangdan, the ten entirely powerful, and the power of this sacred sentence is supposed to be increased by its being written in this form.
